test: Join invoices (2016-2024 invoice dates, to avoid end-cap on due_on) to payments; compute days late = paid_on - due_on in working days and in calendar days, and also against calendar-day terms (invoice date + terms_days calendar) to check whether the working-day conversion of due_on manufactures lateness. Weight by invoice amount. Rank customers by overdue dollar-days; measure share of top 10%/top 28 customers; check year-to-year persistence (rank correlation of customer lateness across years, share of top-decile customers staying top-decile). Break down by segment, terms, invoice size, month. Size excess AR = sum(amount x days late)/days per year and carrying cost at an assumed 8%; size short payments by customer.
support: A minority (<15%) of customers holds >50% of overdue dollar-days; their lateness persists across years (high year-to-year correlation); lateness is substantial even against calendar-day terms; short payments concentrate in the same customers.
weaken: Overdue dollar-days spread roughly in proportion to revenue; most lateness is a few days that disappears when due dates are measured as calendar-day terms; customer lateness ranks don't persist; or one year dominates.
expect: Moderately confident (~60%) that lateness is customer-persistent (payment habits are usually sticky), but the q95 figure of 28 customers holding 0.412 is not 'most', so concentration may be weaker than stated. I expect part of the 18.1 day average to be an artefact: 30 calendar days = 21 working days is fair, but if days late are computed in calendar days against a working-day due date the gap may inflate. Expect the carrying cost to land in the ~$0.1M/yr range, a modest amount.
